transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for fitting me in, I really appreciate it. Am I sitting in the right spot? 

Um... I hope I'm explaining this right, but I came in because... well, I just feel like I've got this motor running inside me all day. It's not that I'm trying to be a bother or anything, I promise. It's just, if I have to sit still—like when I'm at church, or waiting out there in the clinic, or even just sitting around at home—I start feeling kind of trapped? Like I just absolutely have to get up or do something with my hands. 

Does that make sense? I hope that's an okay reason to be here.
When you have this restless feeling and need to move around, do you also find it hard to focus or keep your attention on one thing, or do you feel more worried and anxious?

Oh, well... I wouldn't say I feel worried or anxious, exactly. It's more like... um, I really hope this doesn't make me sound rude, because I swear I'm trying my best to be respectful when people talk to me. I don't ever want to be a burden on anybody. 

But, like, when folks are going over things with me... you know, like ride times, or what we need on the pantry list, or plans for church... I listen real good at the start. I really do. But then... I don't know, my mind just sort of slips off somewhere else without me meaning it to. And then I end up missing pieces of what they said, pieces I really needed to hear. 

I always feel awful about it. Is that... does that answer what you were asking, doctor? I hope I'm not making a mess of explaining things.

How far back do you remember having these troubles with sitting still and keeping your attention? Did this start when you were younger, like in school, or is this something more recent that's come up in your adult life?

Well, um... I guess it's been going on for a real long time. I don't want to make it sound like I was a bad kid or anything, because I really did try to be good for my teachers. I always wanted them to be happy with me. 

But, back when I was a boy in school... well, the teachers, they were always having to move my seat around. I just... I had a really hard time staying put in my chair. And sometimes I'd talk when I wasn't supposed to, or I'd get a little too eager and jump up before the class was officially over. I'd get in trouble for it, and I always felt just terrible afterwards. I never meant to be disruptive, I promise. 

I hope that's the kind of information you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right answers.

You mentioned jumping up before class was over and talking out of turn. Besides those things, do you find yourself doing things without thinking first—like interrupting people, making quick decisions you later regret, or acting on impulses—and does this happen pretty often in your daily life now?

Oh, goodness... um... I really, really hate to admit this, because I was always taught to have good manners. I swear I don't ever do it on purpose to be disrespectful. 

But... yes. Sometimes I do. I just get so eager to help or to be part of the conversation, and I kind of... well, I jump right in with an answer before folks are even done talking. Like with the pastor at church, or my cousin, or even the nice lady down at the food pantry. They'll be right in the middle of saying something, and the words just pop right out of my mouth. 

And then, almost right after, I realize I answered the completely wrong thing because I didn't wait to hear the whole question. Or I can see on their face that I made them mad by cutting them off. I always apologize right away, I really do, because I feel just awful about it. 

Is that... does that make sense for what you were asking, doctor? I hope that doesn't make me sound like a terrible person.

When you think about your biggest challenges right now—the things that cause you the most trouble in your day-to-day life—would you say it's more the difficulty paying attention and staying focused, or is it more the restlessness and the impulses to interrupt and move around?

Oh, um... that's a tough one. I really try not to let any of it cause too much trouble, you know? I do my best to keep it all under control so I'm not bothering anybody. 

But if I had to say which one is the biggest challenge... I guess... maybe the restlessness? And the blurting things out. I just... I hate feeling like I'm stepping on people's toes or being a nuisance when I can't sit still or when I interrupt. The focusing part is hard, too, but I can usually just ask folks to repeat themselves, and they're usually real forgiving about it. But when I interrupt or get antsy, I feel like I'm actively being a bother, and I just can't stand the thought of upsetting anyone. 

Does that sound right? I mean, I hope I'm answering this the way you need me to. I just want to make sure I'm giving you a clear picture without sounding like I'm complaining too much.

When you're trying to do something that requires you to concentrate—like reading a letter, following instructions, or working on a task—how often would you say you actually lose focus or have trouble keeping your mind on it, compared to how often you feel the need to move around or interrupt?

Well, um... I guess it happens sometimes, but I really do try my absolute best to pay attention, I promise. It's just... well, like when the folks at the food pantry are going over the list of what's available, or when we're talking about church plans, or even when someone's just explaining the times for a ride... I start out listening real good. I look right at them and try to catch every word. 

But then, somehow... my mind just sort of slips off. I don't even realize it's happening, and suddenly I've missed pieces of what they were saying. Important pieces that I really needed to hear. I always feel so bad asking them to go over it again, because I know they're busy and I don't want to waste their time. 

Compared to the fidgeting and interrupting, though... I'd say the moving around definitely happens more often, or at least it feels like it causes more of a fuss. The losing focus... it's there, but I really hope it doesn't make me seem like I don't care about what people are saying, because I truly do. 

Does that... is that the kind of example you were looking for? I just want to be sure I'm explaining it right for you.

When you're at home or at work, on a typical day, how many times would you say you have trouble finishing something you started—like not completing a task, a chore, or even a conversation—because your mind wandered or you got distracted?

Oh, um... I really try my best to get everything done that folks ask of me, I really do. I hate to let anybody down. But... well, I guess it does happen more than I'd like to admit. I don't know an exact number of times a day, but it's enough to make me feel pretty bad about it. 

Like, I'll start an errand for my relative, or I'll be given a job to do down at the pantry. And I always start off real strong, you know? I'll get the very first part done just fine. But then... I don't know, my mind just goes somewhere else, and I end up completely forgetting the rest of it. I don't ever leave it half-done on purpose, I swear. But then people find out later that I never actually finished what I started, and I have to apologize all over again. I just worry so much that they'll think I'm lazy or that I don't care about helping them, but it's just that the rest of the job slipped right out of my head. 

I hope that answers your question okay, doctor. I'm trying to be as honest as I can without making it sound like I'm completely unreliable. Is that the kind of thing you were asking about?

You've mentioned that the restlessness and interrupting bother you more, but I want to make sure I understand the full picture. On a typical day right now, would you say you have more trouble with sitting still and the urge to move around, or do you have more trouble with things like losing track of what you're doing, forgetting tasks, or having a hard time organizing things you need to do?

Oh, um... well, I really do try to keep everything straight, I promise I do. I don't want you to think I'm just letting things fall apart on purpose. I do my very best to keep track of it all.

But... if I'm being completely honest, the organizing part... it's a real struggle for me. I guess maybe it is just as bad as the moving around, if I really think about it. It's just... well, my papers, my appointment cards, the food boxes from the pantry, the little notes I try to keep on my phone... they all just get so mixed up. I look at it all, and I just can't figure out what needs doing first. And then, before I know it, everything is already late or I've messed something up entirely. 

I hate it, I really do. I feel awful when I miss an appointment or mix up a box because I couldn't get my things in order. I try so hard to be helpful and stay on top of things, but it just gets so jumbled up in my head and in my space. 

Does that make sense? I hope I'm not making it sound like I'm completely helpless, because I really do try. Is that what you were asking about, doctor?

When you think back over the past few months, would you say the trouble with organizing things, losing track of tasks, and forgetting what you need to do causes you just as much difficulty in your daily life as the fidgeting and interrupting, or does one of them really cause you more problems than the other?

Well, um... I guess they both just kind of pile up and cause a lot of trouble. I really hate to admit this, because I try so hard to be a good helper, I really do. But... if I'm being completely honest... it's gotten to where folks at church, and down at the pantry, and even my own family... they've sort of stopped trusting me with things. 

Like, they don't ask me to handle the food supplies anymore, or help out with the rides, or keep up with the appointments. I think all the forgetting and the jumping around just got to be too much for them to rely on me. I feel like I just keep letting everybody down, even when I truly, truly mean to help and do a good job. I promise I don't do it on purpose, it just... slips away from me. 

I don't want you to think I'm a bad person or that I don't care. I just mess it up despite trying my absolute best. Did I explain that okay for you, doctor? I just want to make sure I'm answering exactly what you need.

When you look back at your whole day—from morning to night—do you spend more time dealing with the fidgeting and needing to move around and interrupt people, or do you spend more time struggling with losing focus, forgetting things, and getting disorganized?

Oh, um... wow, looking at the whole day... that's a tough one to measure, I guess. I really try to just take it as it comes and do my best, you know? 

I... I honestly don't know if I spend more hours on one or the other. It's sort of like they're both just there all the time, kind of mixed together. Like, I might be moving around too much while I'm also forgetting what I was supposed to be doing. I haven't really kept a clock on which one takes up more of my day, if that makes sense. 

I'm sorry I can't give you a better answer on which one is worse time-wise. I hope that's okay, doctor. I really wish I could be more specific for you... is it alright if I just don't know for sure?
When you think about a typical day, do you find yourself more often losing focus and forgetting things, or more often feeling restless and interrupting people?

Well, um... I guess if I had to pick which one happens more often... maybe it's the losing focus part? I really try to pay attention, I promise I do. I want to be respectful and listen to people. 

But... like, when the folks at church are talking through the ride times, or we're going over the pantry lists, or figuring out the plans for the week... I start out listening real good. I'm right there with them. But then... I don't know, my mind just sort of slips off somewhere else. And before I know it, I've missed pieces of what they were saying, things I really needed to hear to do my job right. 

I feel so bad when I have to ask them to repeat it, or when I mess up because I missed a detail. I don't want them to think I don't care about what they're saying, because I really do. I just... I can't seem to hold onto it for very long. 

Does that answer your question better, doctor? I hope I'm giving you what you need to know. I'm really trying to be helpful.

You've mentioned both the trouble focusing and the restlessness. When you're sitting down trying to do something that needs your full attention—like reading something important or following step-by-step instructions—how often during a typical week would you say you struggle to keep your mind on it, compared to how often you feel that urge to get up and move around?

Well, um... when it comes to sitting down for something important, I... I guess the moving around part happens a whole lot. Maybe even more than the focus part, if I really think about it. 

I try so hard to just sit still and be good, especially when I'm supposed to be paying attention. But... like, if I'm in a meeting at church, or even just sitting at the table for a meal, or waiting at the doctor's office... I just get this feeling in my legs. It's like I have to get up. 

I'll make up little excuses, you know? Like, I'll stand up to go get a glass of water, or I'll say I need to check something outside... just so I can move around a little bit. And I know I shouldn't, because everybody else is just sitting there nicely, and then they all look at me... and I feel so embarrassed. I really don't mean to be disruptive or rude. I just can't seem to stay in my chair like a normal person. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound too difficult, doctor. I really am trying to do better with it. Did that make sense? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of examples.

Over the past few months, when you think about what causes you the most problems and gets you into the most trouble—the difficulty paying attention and remembering things, or the restlessness and interrupting—which one would you say is the bigger issue for you?

Oh, um... the biggest issue? Gosh, I... I hate to admit it, because I really do try to be helpful and do things right. But... I think it's all the moving around and the interrupting that gets me into the most trouble. It just... it causes a lot of hurt feelings, and I feel terrible about it.

It's gotten to where... well, the folks at church, and the people running the pantry... even my own family... they've sort of stopped trusting me with things. Like, they won't ask me to help coordinate rides anymore, or keep track of appointments, or handle the supplies. I'll jump in to try and help, or I'll blurt something out while they're organizing, and I just end up making a mess of it. 

They don't say it mean, but I can tell they'd rather I just step back. I feel like I keep letting everybody down, even when I really, truly just mean to help out. I want to be useful to them, I promise I do. It just... it doesn't come out right. 

I'm so sorry if that sounds like I'm a burden on everyone. I really am trying to be better about it. Is that the kind of thing you were asking about, doctor? I hope I'm explaining it okay.

When you think about the last month or two, if you had to choose one thing to work on first to make your life go better—would it be learning to sit still and not interrupt people, or would it be learning to pay better attention and remember things you need to do?

Oh, um... if I had to pick just one to work on first... I think I'd really want to fix the interrupting part. I mean, I try so hard to be helpful and show everyone I'm engaged, but... well, I end up jumping in with an answer before people are even finished talking. 

Like, the pastor, or my cousin, or the pantry lady... they'll be explaining something, and I just blurt out an answer because I get so eager to help out. But then... I realize I answered the wrong thing completely, or I just ended up making them mad because I didn't let them finish their sentence. I feel awful when I make them mad. I really just want them to like having me around, and I hate that I upset them when I'm just trying to be a good listener. 

So I think fixing that would make things a lot better for everybody. Does that sound like a good place to start, doctor? I want to focus on whatever you think is best, I really do.

doctor.intent: Determine whether inattention symptoms are present and impairing, to differentiate between F90.1 (ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type) and F90.0 (ADHD, predominantly inattentive type). doctor.question: When you're at home or at work, on a typical day, how many times would you say you have trouble finishing something you started—like not completing a task, a chore, or even a conversation—because your mind wandered or you got distracted?

target_item.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I’ll start an errand for my relative or a job at the pantry, but I end up doing the first part and then forget the rest, so people find out later that I never finished it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my difficulty finishing tasks, chores, or things I started, which directly corresponds to failing to follow through on instructions or finishing duties.

patient.answer:
Oh, um... I really try my best to get everything done that folks ask of me, I really do. I hate to let anybody down. But... well, I guess it does happen more than I'd like to admit. I don't know an exact number of times a day, but it's enough to make me feel pretty bad about it. 

Like, I'll start an errand for my relative, or I'll be given a job to do down at the pantry. And I always start off real strong, you know? I'll get the very first part done just fine. But then... I don't know, my mind just goes somewhere else, and I end up completely forgetting the rest of it. I don't ever leave it half-done on purpose, I swear. But then people find out later that I never actually finished what I started, and I have to apologize all over again. I just worry so much that they'll think I'm lazy or that I don't care about helping them, but it's just that the rest of the job slipped right out of my head. 

I hope that answers your question okay, doctor. I'm trying to be as honest as I can without making it sound like I'm completely unreliable. Is that the kind of thing you were asking about?

doctor.intent: Differentiate between F90.1 (ADHD Hyperactive-Impulsive Type) and F90.0 (ADHD Inattentive Type) by determining whether inattention symptoms are as prominent or more prominent than hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms in the patient's current presentation.
doctor.question: You've mentioned that the restlessness and interrupting bother you more, but I want to make sure I understand the full picture. target_item.name: Organization_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: My papers, appointment cards, food boxes, and phone notes get all mixed up, and I can’t figure what needs doing first until everything is already late or messed up.
target_item.reason: The doctor asks about having a hard time organizing things needed to do, which directly corresponds to the organization difficulty symptom.

patient.answer:
Oh, um... well, I really do try to keep everything straight, I promise I do. I don't want you to think I'm just letting things fall apart on purpose. I do my very best to keep track of it all.

But... if I'm being completely honest, the organizing part... it's a real struggle for me. I guess maybe it is just as bad as the moving around, if I really think about it. It's just... well, my papers, my appointment cards, the food boxes from the pantry, the little notes I try to keep on my phone... they all just get so mixed up. I look at it all, and I just can't figure out what needs doing first. And then, before I know it, everything is already late or I've messed something up entirely. 

I hate it, I really do. I feel awful when I miss an appointment or mix up a box because I couldn't get my things in order. I try so hard to be helpful and stay on top of things, but it just gets so jumbled up in my head and in my space. 

Does that make sense? I hope I'm not making it sound like I'm completely helpless, because I really do try. Is that what you were asking about, doctor?

doctor.intent: Determine whether inattention symptoms are as prominent and impairing as hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms, which would help differentiate between F90.0 (predominantly inattentive type) and F90.1 (predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type)
doctor.question: When you think back over the past few months, would you say the trouble with organizing things, losing track of tasks, and forgetting what you need to do causes you just as much difficulty in your daily life as the fidgeting and interrupting, or does one of them really cause you more problems than the other?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: People at church, the pantry, and in my family have stopped trusting me with rides, appointments, and supplies, and I feel like I keep letting everybody down even when I mean to help.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the level of difficulty and problems these symptoms cause in the patient's daily life, which corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, um... I guess they both just kind of pile up and cause a lot of trouble. I really hate to admit this, because I try so hard to be a good helper, I really do. But... if I'm being completely honest... it's gotten to where folks at church, and down at the pantry, and even my own family... they've sort of stopped trusting me with things. 

Like, they don't ask me to handle the food supplies anymore, or help out with the rides, or keep up with the appointments. I think all the forgetting and the jumping around just got to be too much for them to rely on me. I feel like I just keep letting everybody down, even when I truly, truly mean to help and do a good job. I promise I don't do it on purpose, it just... slips away from me. 

I don't want you to think I'm a bad person or that I don't care. I just mess it up despite trying my absolute best. Did I explain that okay for you, doctor? I just want to make sure I'm answering exactly what you need.

doctor.intent: Determine whether inattention symptoms are more prominent than hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms, which would indicate F90.0 (Predominantly Inattentive Type) versus F90.1 (Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type)
doctor.question: When you look back at your whole day—from morning to night—do you spend more time dealing with the fidgeting and needing to move around and interrupt people, or do you spend more time struggling with losing focus, forgetting things, and getting disorganized?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking the patient to compare the frequency of hyperactive/impulsive symptoms versus inattentive symptoms to determine the predominant presentation, which does not map to any single specific symptom in the provided profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, um... wow, looking at the whole day... that's a tough one to measure, I guess. I really try to just take it as it comes and do my best, you know? 

I... I honestly don't know if I spend more hours on one or the other. It's sort of like they're both just there all the time, kind of mixed together. Like, I might be moving around too much while I'm also forgetting what I was supposed to be doing. I haven't really kept a clock on which one takes up more of my day, if that makes sense. 

I'm sorry I can't give you a better answer on which one is worse time-wise. I hope that's okay, doctor. I really wish I could be more specific for you... is it alright if I just don't know for sure?

doctor.intent: Determine whether inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity is the predominant presentation by asking about the relative frequency of inattentive symptoms versus hyperactive-impulsive symptoms across the day.
doctor.question: When you think about a typical day, do you find yourself more often losing focus and forgetting things, or more often feeling restless and interrupting people?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When folks are talking through ride times, pantry lists, or church plans, I listen good at first, but then my mind slips off and I miss pieces I really needed to hear.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's tendency to lose focus, which directly maps to difficulty sustaining attention.

patient.answer:
Well, um... I guess if I had to pick which one happens more often... maybe it's the losing focus part? I really try to pay attention, I promise I do. I want to be respectful and listen to people. 

But... like, when the folks at church are talking through the ride times, or we're going over the pantry lists, or figuring out the plans for the week... I start out listening real good. I'm right there with them. But then... I don't know, my mind just sort of slips off somewhere else. And before I know it, I've missed pieces of what they were saying, things I really needed to hear to do my job right. 

I feel so bad when I have to ask them to repeat it, or when I mess up because I missed a detail. I don't want them to think I don't care about what they're saying, because I really do. I just... I can't seem to hold onto it for very long. 

Does that answer your question better, doctor? I hope I'm giving you what you need to know. I'm really trying to be helpful.

doctor.intent: Determine whether inattention symptoms are more prominent than hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms, to differentiate between F90.0 (Predominantly Inattentive Type) and F90.1 (Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type)
doctor.question: You've mentioned both the trouble focusing and the restlessness. When you're sitting down trying to do something that needs your full attention—like reading something important or following step-by-step instructions—how often during a typical week would you say you struggle to keep your mind on it, compared to how often you feel that urge to get up and move around?

target_item.name: Leaving_Seat
target_item.manifestation: In meetings, meals, and waiting rooms, I keep standing up to get water, check outside, or move around, even when everybody else is sitting and looking at me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the urge to get up and move around when expected to stay seated, which directly matches the symptom of leaving one's seat.

patient.answer:
Well, um... when it comes to sitting down for something important, I... I guess the moving around part happens a whole lot. Maybe even more than the focus part, if I really think about it. 

I try so hard to just sit still and be good, especially when I'm supposed to be paying attention. But... like, if I'm in a meeting at church, or even just sitting at the table for a meal, or waiting at the doctor's office... I just get this feeling in my legs. It's like I have to get up. 

I'll make up little excuses, you know? Like, I'll stand up to go get a glass of water, or I'll say I need to check something outside... just so I can move around a little bit. And I know I shouldn't, because everybody else is just sitting there nicely, and then they all look at me... and I feel so embarrassed. I really don't mean to be disruptive or rude. I just can't seem to stay in my chair like a normal person. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound too difficult, doctor. I really am trying to do better with it. Did that make sense? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of examples.

doctor.intent: Determine whether inattention symptoms are more prominent than hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms to differentiate between F90.0 (Predominantly Inattentive Type) and F90.1 (Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type)
doctor.question: Over the past few months, when you think about what causes you the most problems and gets you into the most trouble—the difficulty paying attention and remembering things, or the restlessness and interrupting—which one would you say is the bigger issue for you?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: People at church, the pantry, and in my family have stopped trusting me with rides, appointments, and supplies, and I feel like I keep letting everybody down even when I mean to help.

patient.answer:
Oh, um... the biggest issue? Gosh, I... I hate to admit it, because I really do try to be helpful and do things right. But... I think it's all the moving around and the interrupting that gets me into the most trouble. It just... it causes a lot of hurt feelings, and I feel terrible about it.

It's gotten to where... well, the folks at church, and the people running the pantry... even my own family... they've sort of stopped trusting me with things. Like, they won't ask me to help coordinate rides anymore, or keep track of appointments, or handle the supplies. I'll jump in to try and help, or I'll blurt something out while they're organizing, and I just end up making a mess of it. 

They don't say it mean, but I can tell they'd rather I just step back. I feel like I keep letting everybody down, even when I really, truly just mean to help out. I want to be useful to them, I promise I do. It just... it doesn't come out right. 

I'm so sorry if that sounds like I'm a burden on everyone. I really am trying to be better about it. Is that the kind of thing you were asking about, doctor? I hope I'm explaining it okay.

doctor.intent: Determine whether inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity is the predominant presentation. F90.1 (predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type) would show more hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms causing greater impairment, while F90.0 (predominantly inattentive type) would show more inattention symptoms causing greater impairment. The patient has been somewhat inconsistent, but I need to clarify which symptom cluster is actually causing more functional impairment in their current life.
doctor.question: When you think about the last month or two, if you had to choose one thing to work on first to make your life go better—would it be learning to sit still and not interrupt people, or would it be learning to pay better attention and remember things you need to do?

target_item.name: Blurting_Answers
target_item.manifestation: I jump in with an answer before the pastor, my cousin, or the pantry lady is done talking, and then I realize I answered the wrong thing or made them mad.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking which set of symptoms the patient wants to work on first, specifically mentioning 'interrupting people'. The patient can use the manifestation for blurting out answers/interrupting to address this.

patient.answer:
Oh, um... if I had to pick just one to work on first... I think I'd really want to fix the interrupting part. I mean, I try so hard to be helpful and show everyone I'm engaged, but... well, I end up jumping in with an answer before people are even finished talking. 

Like, the pastor, or my cousin, or the pantry lady... they'll be explaining something, and I just blurt out an answer because I get so eager to help out. But then... I realize I answered the wrong thing completely, or I just ended up making them mad because I didn't let them finish their sentence. I feel awful when I make them mad. I really just want them to like having me around, and I hate that I upset them when I'm just trying to be a good listener. 

So I think fixing that would make things a lot better for everybody. Does that sound like a good place to start, doctor? I want to focus on whatever you think is best, I really do.

inference.note: Patient demonstrates predominant hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms (restlessness, interrupting, difficulty staying seated, blurting out answers) as the primary concern causing functional impairment. While inattention is present, the patient consistently identifies hyperactivity and impulsivity as the main issues affecting relationships and daily functioning. This pattern is most consistent with ADHD, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type (F90.1) rather than the Combined Type (F90.0). Symptoms began in childhood, persist into adulthood, and cause significant social and occupational difficulties.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a long-standing history of hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms (restlessness, difficulty sitting still, interrupting, blurting out answers) that began in childhood and persist into adulthood. While inattention is also present (losing focus, forgetting tasks, disorganization), the patient consistently identifies hyperactivity-impulsivity as the more prominent and functionally impairing domain. The patient explicitly states that interrupting and restlessness cause more trouble and get more negative reactions from others, and prioritizes addressing these symptoms. Symptoms have caused documented functional impairment (loss of trusted responsibilities at church, pantry, and family). F90.1 (ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type) is the best fit, though F90.0 (predominantly inattentive type) remains a close differential given the significant attention difficulties acknowledged.
